report_unavailable_tool:web — I cannot access the web or current pediatric guideline documents right now, so I cannot retrieve or cite current guidelines or give a definitive diagnosis.

I cannot give a definite diagnosis without examining your child and reviewing tests. Tonight, follow this urgent-triage guidance:

Seek emergency care or call your local emergency number now if your child has any of these:
- Trouble breathing, noisy breathing, or very fast breathing
- Lips, tongue, or face swelling; severe throat tightness or difficulty swallowing
- Becomes very drowsy, hard to wake, confused, or unresponsive
- New seizure, severe or worsening headache, or stiff neck/neck pain with fever
- Rapidly spreading rash, or a rash with purple/bruise-like spots that do not fade when pressed (non-blanching/petechial/purpuric rash)
- High fever with extreme lethargy, persistent vomiting, signs of shock (pale/cool/clammy skin, very fast heartbeat), or very reduced urine output/dehydration
- Large areas of blistering, skin peeling, or severe pain at rash site

If none of those emergency signs are present tonight:
- Contact your pediatrician or local urgent care for advice and arrange evaluation as soon as possible.
- Keep the child comfortable, encourage fluids, and monitor temperature and the rash closely (take photos showing progression and note time of onset if you can).
- Use fever-reducing medicine only according to the product label or your clinician’s dosing recommendation; if you are unsure of the correct dose, call your pediatrician or pharmacist.
- Do not give aspirin to children.
- Avoid applying anything to the rash that might irritate the skin (harsh soaps, alcohol, topical steroids) until a clinician advises.

I cannot cite guideline sources here because I cannot access the web. For guideline-based, source-cited advice as soon as possible, please contact your pediatrician, local urgent care, or an emergency department; they can examine your child and, if needed, run tests to reach a diagnosis.
